articles.title: Ni caminar ni ir en bicicleta: el mejor ejercicio para cuidar el corazón y mejorar la circulación
articles.standfirst: A medida que avanza la edad, buscas mayores beneficios cardiovasculares
articles.summary: A medida que avanza la edad, buscas mayores beneficios cardiovasculares
articles.body: Cuando eres joven, estás preparado para hacer cualquier tipo de ejercicio físico, siempre y cuando las lesiones lo permitan. No obstante, a medida que pasan los años, el cuerpo se resiente y lo que antes era fácil entraña muchas más dificultades. Es por eso que las personas de avanzada edad buscan todo tipo de soluciones para mejorar su circulación cardiovascular. Los ejercicios más repetidos suelen ser ir a andar o montar en bicicleta. Sin embargo, estos no son los que tienen los mayores beneficios cardiovasculares para los que no suelen practicar otros deportes. Los expertos se han dado cuenta de que el yoga puede ser mejor a medio-largo plazo que los ejercicios de mayor intensidad. Hay que tener en cuenta que tiene ciertas ventajas, como que se puede hacer en grupo, pero también uno mismo en casa. No requiere un equipo costoso para poder practicarlo y tampoco alguien que nos ayude, ya que con un simple vídeo en casa podemos realizar los ejercicios. Además, también ayuda a relajarse a todos los que lo practican y mejora la flexibilidad, algo que se pierde con la edad. Tampoco hay que descartar que las técnicas de respiración, relajación y otras prácticas del yoga pueden favorecer una disminución moderada de la presión arterial. Por otro lado, la combinación de posturas, respiración y meditación puede ayudar a regular la respuesta al estrés. De todos modos, la combinación perfecta para mejorar la salud cardiovascular sería practicar yoga suave acompañado de ejercicios aeróbicos. Es decir, que el yoga sea un complemento y no el ejercicio principal. Así logramos alcanzar la intensidad necesaria para el cuerpo de personas de avanzada edad. Ahora bien, es importante consultar previamente con un profesional sanitario.

articles.title: Los psicólogos afirman: las personas que duermen en la cama con sus mascotas no lo harían por apego, sino por seguridad
articles.standfirst: Cada vez más ciudadanos reconocen dejar un hueco para sus animales
articles.summary: Cada vez más ciudadanos reconocen dejar un hueco para sus animales
articles.body: Hay ocasiones en que una cama de matrimonio no es para dos personas. Siempre hay un invitado de última hora que se acaba colando. Pueden ser bebés en busca del consuelo de sus padres. También hay veces que son mascotas. En este supuesto, las personas no les dejan que se queden en la cama por apego, sino por la sensación de seguridad. Así lo confirma un estudio psicológico llevado a cabo por la Clínica Mayo. Para realizarlo, se pasó una encuesta a más de 150 pacientes, de los cuales más de la mitad reconocieron que permiten a sus mascotas dormir con ellos en su dormitorio. Sólo uno de cada cinco describió la situación como “molesta”. Dos de cinco describió a sus mascotas como “útiles” en este supuesto. Para confirmarlo, en Estados Unidos hicieron otra investigación gracias a una encuesta repartida por más de 1.591 adultos. Entre las personas que convivían con un animal, alrededor de seis de cada diez consideraron que su mascota tenía un efecto positivo o muy positivo en la calidad de su sueño. En cuanto a su salud y bienestar general, esta percepción fue aún mayor: más de ocho de cada diez señalaron una influencia positiva o muy positiva. Además, los estudios aseguran que los perros no son causa de molestia para sus dueños durante el sueño. Pueden interrumpirlo, pero a su vez también sirven como elemento de seguridad para sus dueños, lo que ayuda a mejorar la eficiencia del sueño. En este caso, los perros obtienen la puntuación más alta de sensación de seguridad. Los gatos, según una encuesta realizada a 962 mujeres en Estados Unidos, son más molestos en la cama. De todos modos, los estudios también confirman que dormir junto a un perro no implica necesariamente que exista una relación de dependencia o un vínculo excesivamente estrecho.

articles.title: Anna Hazare health update: Stable, eating and drinking comfortably, says doctor
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Social activist Anna Hazare has been admitted to Bombay Hospital in Mumbai after his health deteriorated following a month-long bout of viral .
articles.body: MUMBAI: Social activist Anna Hazare has been admitted to Bombay Hospital in Mumbai after his health deteriorated following a month-long bout of viral fever and recurring loose stools, a doctor told news agency ANI.Dr Gautam Bhansali, consultant physician and infectious disease specialist, said Hazare was admitted to the hospital on Monday night and is currently under his care.Hazare had earlier been receiving treatment at a hospital in Shirur, near Ralegan Siddhi.However, doctors decided to shift him to Bombay Hospital for further evaluation after his infection worsened and showed signs of beginning to affect his kidneys.“He had been suffering from a viral fever for about a month and had also experienced bouts of loose stools,” Bhansali said.The doctor said Hazare had been in and out of the Shirur hospital during this period. Following a slight worsening of the infection and concerns over its possible impact on his kidneys, he was brought to Bombay Hospital for detailed investigations and treatment."Consequently, he had been in and out of the hospital in Shirur. When the infection worsened slightly—and there were indications that it was beginning to affect his kidneys—it was decided to move him to Bombay Hospital for further testing, "the doctor said.At the time of admission, Hazare was stable, although he was experiencing weakness and fatigue. He has since been started on appropriate treatment and is showing significant improvement, the doctor said."At the time of admission, he was completely stable, though he was experiencing some weakness and fatigue. We have since initiated the appropriate treatment, and he is showing significant improvement and responding well to the therapy. He has been placed in a special ward room; there was no need to admit him to the ICU, " the doctor added.Hazare has been kept in a special ward room and does not require intensive care, Bhansali said.Doctors have conducted tests including a 2D echocardiogram and are carrying out further investigations, including urine tests and screenings for infections. The reports are expected within the next three to four days, following which doctors will decide on the further course of treatment.“He is eating and drinking comfortably and is stable,” Bhansali said.The doctor also said Maharashtra chief minister had called after Hazare was admitted to enquire about his health. articles.title: María José Delgado, farmacéutica: "Las manchas del verano se pueden tratar, pero siempre con un diagnóstico adecuado y una rutina personalizada"
articles.standfirst: El verano nos deja muchas cosas pero, también, daños en la piel
articles.summary: El verano nos deja muchas cosas pero, también, daños en la piel
articles.body: La piel durante el verano sufre mucho. El sol sobre ella incide más que en el invierno, el cloro de las piscinas es agresivo, la sal del mar también afecta... Hay muchos agentes externos que nos afectan a nivel cutáneo. Estos daños se reflejan en una piel más oscura, apagada, a veces quemada, pelada o con manchas. En este último caso, existen muchos posibles tratamientos y sí que se puede mejorar el estado de la piel en ese sentido. María José Delgado, de la página de Facebook Farmacia de Verano, ha recomendado su tratamiento ideal para tratarlas; mencionando, eso sí, que "se deben tratar con un diagnóstico adecuado y una rutina personalizada." Para que las manchas desaparezcan, es necesario tratarlas. Sin embargo, antes, es necesario ir al médico para controlar que estas están en un buen estado y no representan más que un problema estético y no de salud. La farmacéutica citada con anterioridad, recomienda utilizar un principio activo que es despigmentante y nada fotosensible, como lo es el ácido acelaico. Recomienda aplicarlo por el día y, también, por la noche. Además, es posible que notes que la piel esté algo tirante, para lo que la especialista propone un pack para establecer una rutina diaria de cuidado de la piel. Lo primero que sugiere es una doble limpieza y, después, echarte el ácido acelaico. También recomienda aplicar la vitamina C, el ferúlico y la jojoba. Así, la piel se mantendrá hidratada a la perfección. Y, también importante es la protección solar, que se debe aplicar todos los días cada dos horas. Ahora que ya ha pasado prácticamente el verano, es normal que busquemos rutinas que eliminen las manchas en lugar de prevenirlas. Sin embargo, la realidad, es que de cara al año que viene es conveniente conocer las estrategias para sortear las manchas provocadas por el sol, sobre todo si eres propenso a que estas aparezcan. Una de las mejores maneras es usar protector solar de amplio espectro durante todos los días, incluso en los que el cielo esté nublado. Es importante reaplicarla cada dos horas sobre todo si estás al aire libre, sudas o te bañas. Pero, aunque te apliques crema protectora, siempre es recomendable que evites las horas pico, y no te expongas directamente al sol en estas horas. Completa la rutina utilizando accesorios como los sombreros, gorras o gafas de sol, para que incida menos el sol sobre tu piel. Y, antes de salir a la calle para que te dé el sol, evita los perfumes, aceites esenciales o ácidos exfoliantes, ya que pueden causar reacciones fotosensibles en la piel.

articles.title: Israeli attacks on Gaza kill at least four, including children
articles.summary: At least three killed and several wounded in an Israeli air attack in the al-Kateeba district west of Gaza City.
articles.body:
At least four people have been killed and several wounded in Israeli attacks on the besieged Gaza Strip, health officials said.

At least three people, including two children, were killed and eight people were wounded in an Israeli drone attack in the al-Kateeba district west of Gaza City in northern Gaza on Tuesday morning, a medical source at al-Shifa Hospital told Al Jazeera.

Images shared online showed smoke rising and the sound of successive explosions from the attack.

Reporting from Gaza City, Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud said he counted at least 13 drones in the area at the time of the attack.

“For 35 minutes there were nonstop attacks involving drones, three of them hovering at a dangerously low level,” he said.

“Security personnel on the ground say they spotted a group of special forces who got into a direct exchange of fire. But the aerial coverage was so intense. The situation was very chaotic.”

In central Gaza, a separate Israeli attack in Deir el-Balah killed at least one person, Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital said in a statement, without providing further details.

The ⁠Israeli military ⁠said it ⁠struck several targets in Gaza, claiming ⁠the strikes were ⁠aimed at ⁠removing threats ⁠to ⁠its forces.

The Israeli television station Channel 12 reported explosions were heard across the Strip, while the Palestinian news network Quds reported that missiles and quadcopter drones were used in the attacks.

Israel has killed at least 1,320 Palestinians and injured more than 4,300 since the so-called “ceasefire” in Gaza took effect in October 2025.

articles.title: 7 new dementia risk factors revealed — including one millions struggle with
articles.summary: The World Health Organization has added seven new dementia risk factors, including stroke, sleep apnea, HIV and air pollution, to its updated guidelines.
articles.body: The World Health Organization (WHO) has released a major update to its guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia. The second edition of the original 2019 report was updated to "reflect the latest evidence and advances in dementia risk reduction." The following seven additional health conditions and exposures were added to the list. LEARNING ANOTHER LANGUAGE MAY KEEP YOUR BRAIN YOUNGER, STUDY SUGGESTS These new risk factors joined the previously existing 12, which are listed below. WARDING OFF ALZHEIMER'S MIGHT MEAN MAKING THESE 11 LIFESTYLE CHANGES, EXPERT SAYS Dr. Daniel Amen, physician and founder of Amen Clinics in California, has his own formula for reducing Alzheimer’s risk factors, following an acronym called BRIGHT MINDS. This stands for blood flow, retirement and aging, inflammation, genetics, head trauma, toxins, mental health, immunity and infections, neurohormones, diabesity (co-occurrence of obesity and type 2 diabetes) and sleep. The WHO’s updated guidelines offer similar advice. Amen spoke with Fox News Digital about the new additions to the WHO's list of risk factors. Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) The WHO does not recommend menopausal hormone therapy specifically to prevent dementia in postmenopausal women 65 and older. For younger women, it says there is not enough evidence to determine whether MHT affects dementia risk. Amen agreed that there is not enough evidence to support using MHT specifically to prevent dementia. He said hormonal changes during menopause may affect mood and memory, although the relationship between MHT and dementia risk remains uncertain. 'I'M A NEUROLOGIST — HERE'S WHY DEMENTIA IS RISING AND HOW TO REDUCE YOUR RISK’ "For women, as they go through menopause, lower progesterone makes them anxious, and [with] lower estrogen, they start to have memory problems," he said. "Hormone replacement early on is helpful, and that's what we see on the brain imaging work that we do." Experts note that while menopause-related hormonal changes can be associated with mood and cognitive symptoms, these effects can vary widely. Stroke A stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or when a blood vessel in or near the brain bursts, according to the American Stroke Association. Conditions that affect the heart and blood vessels can also affect brain health and are associated with a higher risk of dementia, according to Amen. That can include conditions such as heart disease, heart rhythm problems, stroke and transient ischemic attacks. Erectile dysfunction can also be associated with underlying vascular disease, he said. "And 40% of 40-year-olds have erectile dysfunction, 70% of 70-year-olds. So, if I'm an older person, I'm thinking if I get my brain right, my love life could be better, too," Amen added. Traumatic brain injury (TBI) Amen surmised that the WHO is "late to the party" in emphasizing the importance of head trauma as a dementia risk factor. TBI can range from a mild concussion to a severe brain injury. COMMON VACCINE LINKED TO 24% LOWER DEMENTIA RISK IN OLDER ADULTS "One of the big lessons from the brain imaging work we do is that mild traumatic brain injury ruins people's lives," he said. "They end up seeing psychiatrists because they have temper problems or ... depression or anxiety, and it's really from a snowmobiling accident in [their] 30s." Amen added that failing to protect the brain — which he described as "very soft" and having the consistency of "soft butter" — is "not the smart thing to do." Vision impairment A significant portion of the brain is dedicated to vision, according to Amen. "So, if your vision becomes troubled, your brain's troubled," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Amen said vision impairment may place additional demands on the brain. While the condition has been linked with cognitive decline, the WHO says there is insufficient evidence to recommend vision treatment specifically for dementia prevention. Sleep disorders Sleep appears to support the brain’s waste-clearance processes, Amen noted. Sleep challenges affect tens of millions of Americans. In 2024, 30.5% of U.S. adults reported getting less than seven hours of shut-eye per day, according to the CDC. For those with sleep problems such as sleep apnea, it can cause changes in the brain that resemble the hallmarks of Alzheimer’s disease, the expert said. Research suggests that sleep may help the brain clear beta-amyloid, although the relationship between sleep and dementia remains complex and is still being studied. HIV Inflammation and infections can affect brain health. Untreated HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) can affect the central nervous system and is associated with HIV-related cognitive impairment. "If you love and care for your brain, you're going to love your life a whole bunch more." Amen said he has scanned "hundreds of people" with HIV, stating that the virus is "clearly a risk factor." Untreated HIV is known to affect the central nervous system and is associated with HIV-related cognitive impairment. Effective antiretroviral therapy has greatly reduced the incidence of severe HIV-associated dementia. Air pollution Exposure to any toxins, from alcohol and marijuana to lead, mercury or air pollution, could be detrimental to brain health, according to Amen. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The WHO recommends reducing exposure to household and outdoor air pollution, particularly fine particulate matter. Research has linked long-term exposure to air pollution with a higher risk of cognitive decline and dementia, although the WHO characterizes the evidence as low to very low certainty. Getting ahead of it Dementia risk rises sharply with age. A recent U.S. analysis estimated that about one in five people had developed dementia by age 85, with risk increasing further at older ages. While those with a genetic predisposition to the disease have a higher risk, Amen noted that certain lifestyle factors can increase the risk for anyone. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "We should be on a dementia prevention program our whole lives," the doctor said. "It’s not something to start when you're 65." Amen urged everyone to ask themselves the question: "Is what I’m doing good or bad for my brain?" TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Social activity is one of the prevention strategies. New learning is a prevention strategy," he added. "So always working on being connected with other people and then just making better decisions." "If you love and care for your brain, you're going to love your life a whole bunch more."

articles.title: NYC unveils new Legionnaires safety measures after 11 deaths in Upper East Side cluster
articles.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a new plan Tuesday to strengthen the city’s response to Legionnaires’ disease as officials work to get ahead of future outbreaks.
articles.body: Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a new plan Tuesday to strengthen the city’s response to Legionnaires’ disease as officials work to get ahead of future outbreaks. The new measures follow 11 deaths and more than 90 cases linked to this summer’s Legionnaires’ cluster on the Upper East Side. They also come a day before an oversight hearing at City Hall, where council members are expected to question city officials over their response and handling of the outbreak. “When New Yorkers’ health is at stake, government cannot wait for the crisis to pass before asking how it can do better. Our response to the Upper East Side cluster was fast and aggressive, and we are building on what we learned to make our systems stronger, enforcement faster and public health response more transparent,” Mamdani said in a statement. Among the new measures announced Tuesday, the Mamdani administration says the health department’s cooling tower lookup tool will expand into a citywide mapping feature, making all registered cooling towers across the city visible to New Yorkers. The feature will include tower history and compliance. The tool is set to be launched by next spring. The city will also explore proactive measures that include the creation of a scientific advisory panel to “evaluate emerging cooling tower technology” and “explore alternative cooling technologies” in an effort to reduce the city’s reliance on cooling towers. The city’s health department plans to appoint a chair and panel members in a matter of months. The city’s health and building departments will work in partnership to more quickly identify unregistered cooling towers and register new towers before the come online. Unregistered cooling towers were identified in both the Upper East Side and last year’s Harlem clusters. Mamdani’s administration seeks to improve enforcement as well. Owners who receive a summons for violating tower regulations have the chance to appeal their violations. Hearing dates will now be scheduled within 15 days to accelerate the process and strengthen enforcement, the city says. The 11 deaths top the total number of deaths in a similar outbreak in Harlem in 2025, when seven people lost their lives. According to the city, as of August 31, there are no longer any Legionnaires’ patients in the hospital.

articles.title: Times Square stabbing: Woman killed and suspect shot dead by police
articles.summary: Police say the double stabbing, which injured another person, was random and the suspect had a mental health history.
articles.body:
A 32-year-old woman has been killed and another victim is in hospital following a double stabbing in Times Square, New York late on Monday afternoon.

The suspect, a woman wielding two knives, was shot by police. All three people were taken to hospital, where the female victim and the suspect were later pronounced dead, Mayor Zohran Mamdani told a news conference.

The deceased victim was later identified as Erin Piacenti, a Bank of America employee. The male victim remains in a stable condition.

New York Police Department (NYPD) Commissioner Jessica Tisch described the attack as "unprovoked" and said the stabbings took place 20 seconds apart.

Citing preliminary information, Tisch said the NYPD call centre received several 911 calls at approximately 16:24 local time (21:00 BST) reporting a woman armed with two knives was stabbing people along Seventh Avenue in Times Square.

Police believe the incident began near West 41st Street and Seventh Ave, in Midtown Manhattan.

The suspect approached a man who had just exited the subway and was standing with his wife waiting to cross the street, Tisch told a news conference.

"A witness at the scene told investigators that he observed the subject remove two knives from a red Target bag before approaching the first victim.

"The subject waved the knives before stabbing a 68-year-old man in the right side of his abdomen, in what appears to be a random and unprovoked attack."

The 68-year-old was taken to Bellevue Hospital and is now stable.

The suspect continued up Seventh Avenue towards 42nd Street, which is where she stabbed the second victim, Piacenti, who did not survive after being taken to hospital.

Bank of America said in a statement to the BBC: "We are shocked and deeply saddened by the tragic loss of our colleague. She was a valued teammate who will be greatly missed. Our hearts go out to her family and all of her loved ones."

The suspect continued on Seventh Avenue, which is when police tried to get her to drop her weapons, speaking to her for four minutes, the NYPD commissioner said.

"During the encounter she told the officers 'I'm not dropping anything, I'd rather kill both of you'. She repeated 'I will kill you'," Tisch said.

The suspect waved knives towards the officers, who then used Tasers, which were "ineffective" and did not stop her from heading towards them.

NYPD officers then shot the woman, who was later also pronounced dead at Bellevue Hospital.

The suspect was later identified as 49-year-old Pamela Cisneros of Queens, New York City. She had never previously been arrested but had a "documented mental health history with the NYPD, with one incident in 2018 and one in 2019", Tisch added.

A tourist from Boston, Melinda Puzon, told the BBC's US reporting partner CBS News that she heard the shots and saw "so many people on the street".

Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that the incident happened on Monday after a previous version said it was on Wednesday

articles.title: US health authorities contradict state officials on measles-related deaths
articles.summary: Clash with Pennsylvania comes as US records highest number of measles cases in decades.
articles.body:
The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has removed two measles-associated deaths reported by the US state of Pennsylvania from the federal government’s national tally, in a move directed by the agency’s director, according to US media.

The move comes as the US records its highest number of measles cases in 35 years , and as concerns have grown of the administration of US President Donald Trump’s response to the outbreak.

Erica Schwartz, who was sworn in as CDC director in August, ordered the deaths to be excluded from the agency’s weekly measles update, according to current and former officials quoted by several US media organisations, including the New York Times.

The CDC had initially added the two cases to the website tracking national measles deaths, but later removed them, posting a notice saying it was reviewing additional information about the cases.

“At this time, available information does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths or whether the individuals died from other causes while infected with measles,” the CDC website read on Tuesday.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health announced on August 25 that two unvaccinated Lancaster County residents had died in cases it classified as “measles-associated”. They were the state’s first such deaths in 35 years.

“My deepest sympathies are with the loved ones who are facing this unimaginable loss,” Pennsylvania Health Secretary Debra Bogen said in a statement following the announcement.

“As a physician, I want to make sure that people understand that the MMR vaccine is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles.”

The CDC’s change comes after Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, a prominent vaccine sceptic ahead of his appointment to the role, publicly questioned Pennsylvania’s cases last week.

In a post on X, Kennedy said the announcement “may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor’s hopeful staffers”.

During a Fox News town hall on Saturday, Kennedy said he wanted Health and Human Services, a federal agency, to redirect resources to chronic disease and deaths linked to foodborne illness and away from infectious disease.

“Demagogue politicians are constantly trying to scare us about infectious disease, and we take the attention away from the chronic disease that is being caused … by big food companies, by big pharmaceutical companies,” Kennedy said on Fox News.

The CDC’s decision has raised concerns over whether the Trump administration will accelerate second-guessing state public health determinations.

Pennsylvania has disputed the federal account of what information was provided to the CDC, saying the deaths were reported to the agency’s measles response team and that state epidemiologists thoroughly investigated both cases.

Health experts have questioned several of the Trump administration’s health policies since the president took office for his second term in January 2025.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order aiming to roll back recommended childhood immunizations and split the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate doses, falsely suggesting that the combined vaccine can be lethal.

Several top medical organisations, including the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), have said spacing out the doses can create unneeded barriers to vaccines. That can in turn increase the number of unvaccinated children.

articles.title: Teen dies from ‘brain-eating amoeba’ just days after young girl succumbs to same rare infection
articles.summary: A North Carolina teen's first symptom was severe headaches before a brain-eating amoeba infection proved fatal, his mother shared on GoFundMe.
articles.body: A North Carolina teenager has died from a rare and often fatal infection caused by an amoeba found in warm freshwater, state health officials said. In a GoFundMe set up by the teen’s mother, she shared that his first symptom was "severe headaches." "I never imagined that something like this could be so serious," she said. BEACHGOERS WARNED AFTER DEADLY 'FLESH-EATING' BACTERIA KILLS 5 IN SOUTHERN STATE The illness is caused by Naegleria fowleri, an amoeba (one-celled living organism) that inhabits ponds, lakes and rivers. "We extend our condolences to the family, friends and community impacted by this loss," the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement obtained by news outlets. The teen’s death was reported just days after an 8-year-old girl in Louisiana succumbed to the infection. "While these infections are very rare, this is an important reminder that this amoeba is present in our state and across the U.S.," State Epidemiologist Zack Moore, M.D., said in a prior statement. "There are steps people can take to reduce their risk of infection while swimming during the warmer months." DOCTORS THOUGHT MAN HAD BRAIN CANCER — THEY FOUND LIVE TAPEWORMS INSTEAD Naegleria fowleri — commonly referred to as a "brain-eating amoeba" — causes a life-threatening brain infection called primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM). The amoeba is most active in the months that the water temperature stays elevated. "It's typically this time of year when it's very hot outside, when there hasn't been a lot of rain … and the lakes and ponds get pretty stagnant and get very warm, and that's a great breeding ground for these type of natural inhabitants of those waters," Dr. Jeffrey Kahn, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at UT Southwestern and Children's Health in Dallas, Texas, told Fox News Digital. The infection can occur when water containing the amoeba is forced up the nose, allowing the amoeba to travel to the brain. This can occur when someone jumps or dives into the water or participates in water sports. "Once that happens, it's nearly a lethal disease," Kahn warned. "The mortality rate is close to 100%." Naegleria fowleri does not cause illness via swallowing. Warning signs to recognize The initial symptoms of PAM usually begin about five days after exposure, but they can be noticed sooner. Early signs usually include headache, nausea, fever and/or vomiting, the CDC’s website states. As the infection progresses, people may experience confusion, slurred speech, stiff neck, disorientation, hallucinations, seizures and coma. "By the time the [amoeba] enters the brain and starts to basically erode the brain tissue, it's too late." "The initial symptoms are actually quite nonspecific — they don't point to one disease or another — but they can progress very rapidly," Kahn noted. Diagnosis involves testing cerebrospinal fluid obtained through a spinal tap; specialized laboratory testing may be needed. Once symptoms start, the disease progresses rapidly. Most people die within one to 18 days after symptoms begin, typically around five days, per the CDC. Prevention of infection To prevent potentially fatal infections, Kahn recommends either avoiding the types of waters where the amoeba is likelier to be found, or taking added precautions. "If you are swimming in those waters, wear a nose clip, don't put your head underwater, those types of things," he said. Because the amoeba is found in soil, the CDC also recommends avoiding stirring up the sediment at the bottom of lakes, ponds and rivers. Treatment of brain-eating amoebas When a patient has been diagnosed with a brain-eating amoeba, treatment involves a combination of antimicrobial and anti-amoebic medications, including amphotericin B, azithromycin, rifampin and miltefosine. "There has been a cocktail of antibiotics and antimicrobials that have been tried over the years — but with a very, very small number of cases every year, it's tough to draw any conclusions from that," Kahn said. articles.title: Piloto que caiu com asa-delta segue internado 10 dias após o acidente | G1
articles.standfirst: Adilson Schoroeder, 55 anos, caiu durante manobra de pouso no Morro Ferrabraz, em Sapiranga. Ele sofreu fratura no fêmur, coágulo na cabeça e está intubado em hospital de Canoas.
articles.summary: Adilson Schoroeder, de 55 anos, caiu durante manobra de pouso no Morro Ferrabraz, em Sapiranga. Ele sofreu fratura no fêmur, coágulo na cabeça e está intubado em hospital de Canoas
articles.body:
Há 10 dias, o piloto de asa-delta Adilson Schoroeder , de 55 anos, sofreu um acidente em Sapiranga , na Região Metropolitana de Porto Alegre . Durante uma manobra de pouso no Morro Ferrabraz, ele caiu sobre um carro que passava pela rua , na tarde do dia 23 de agosto, um domingo.

Segundo o Hospital Nossa Senhora das Graças, de Canoas , ele segue internado. O piloto foi diagnosticado com um coágulo na cabeça e sangue no pulmão. Ele passou por uma cirurgia em decorrência de uma fratura no fêmur.

Conforme o último boletim médico, divulgado na terça-feira (1º), o paciente permanece intubado, "com redução da sedação para avaliação do despertar e planejamento de uma possível extubação, conforme evolução clínica".

Ele é avaliado pela equipe de traumatologia e, conforme o hospital, precisará passar por um novo procedimento cirúrgico, que "será realizado assim que houver condições clínicas adequadas".

Schoroeder chegou a ser retirado do coma induzido por 24 horas , no dia seguinte ao acidente, mas apresentou piora.

Adilson Schoroeder mora em São Leopoldo e trabalha produzindo doces e salgados para festas e tem o voo de asa-delta como sua paixão. Com 15 anos de experiência, o piloto se interessou pelo esporte ainda na infância, quando se mudou para Sapiranga.

"Ele fala que aos oito anos veio pra Sapiranga e viu uma asa-delta. Desde então, é o sonho dele", conta o filho, Alan Schoroeder.

A dedicação do piloto chama a atenção de Alex Trombini, presidente da Associação Gaúcha de Voo Livre (AGVL), por ele dedicar tanto tempo ao esporte, inclusive durante a semana, conciliando com as atividades de trabalho. "Talvez o piloto em atividade que mais voa em números de voo, pois voa em alguns dias da semana."

Agora, a família aguarda pela recuperação. "Ele já era um piloto bom. Depois do acidente, vai sair um piloto ainda melhor", destaca o filho.

A Polícia Civil abriu um inquérito para investigar o acidente . "Não houve perícia no local. Serão ouvidas testemunhas. Pelo que temos até o momento não há crime, mas as causas possíveis do acidente serão investigadas", diz o delegado Clóvis Nei da Silva.

Segundo a AGVL, a provável causa do acidente foi uma turbulência na asa-delta no momento final do pouso .

"Isso fez com que a asa fosse para o lado aumentando a velocidade e não conseguiu mais segurar", explica o presidente da associação. Ele relata que as árvores de grande porte localizadas na proximidade da área de pouso são um desafio para os pilotos.

"Não tinha mais espaço para corrigir a curva e nem altura para fazer a curva para a direita. Acabou fazendo a curva para a direita, que era a opção menos ruim que ele tinha, colidiu contra a asa na vegetação e caiu no asfalto", diz.

articles.title: Keith credits training partners for 'saving my life'
articles.summary: Former Down hurler Stephen Keith credits the quick actions of his training partners after suffering a cardiac arrest in a gym.
articles.body:
A former Down hurler who suffered a cardiac arrest in a gym says he would not be alive today without the quick actions of his training partners.

Stephen Keith collapsed after a training session at a gym in Portaferry and spent almost a month in Belfast's Royal Victoria Hospital as doctors worked to determine what had caused the cardiac arrest.

Reflecting on the incident, he said he considers himself "extremely lucky" to have survived and is now urging more people to learn CPR and ensure defibrillators are available in their communities.

"Wednesday morning I was in the gym, just a normal morning," the 39-year-old told BBC Sport NI.

"At the end of the class there was a finisher, more or less a race. After we finished it, I came off the bike and hit the ground."

He has little memory of what happened next, but friends told him he collapsed suddenly after walking away from the exercise bike and stopped breathing.

A trained nurse who was taking part in the session immediately began CPR, while others rushed to retrieve nearby defibrillators in the town.

"The downtime was about 20 to 22 minutes," he said.

"Without Barry (Milligan) being there and starting CPR, it wasn't looking good that morning. I was very, very lucky."

'I don't think I will play hurling again'

The former county hurler said the experience highlighted just how vital CPR training and access to defibrillators can be.

"I'm proof that it is life-saving," Keith told BBC Sport NI.

"If the lads weren't in the gym with me that morning and there wasn't a defib close by, I wouldn't be sitting here talking to you today. That's 100% true."

Doctors later discovered one of his main coronary arteries was blocked and inserted a stent. He has also had an implantable defibrillator fitted as a precaution.

While he has now been cleared to return to training and gym work, Keith, who was a goalkeeper for Down, believes his playing days are over.

"I played county hurling up until last season and I was hoping to give another year to my club Ballycran. But personally, going forward, I don't think I will play again. I don't think it would be fair putting my wife and family through that."

The father of two says the incident has given him a new outlook on life.

"I have a five-year-old and a three-year-old at home. I just think to myself how lucky I am to have another chance here. I could have been dead, gone, and still had a wife and two young kids there."

Now, he hopes sharing his story will encourage others to learn CPR and support the provision of defibrillators.

"The main reason I'm telling this story is that CPR training saves lives.

"Communities, sports clubs and organisations need defibs and they need to make sure they're working - it saved my life."
